title: ReCoG: Relational Concept Graph for Training-Free Personalization
claim: Describing concepts independently yields generic, shared attributes that confuse similar items; conditioning on inter-concept relations elicits discriminative cues that resolve ambiguity.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels split by dashed line, top-down flow, red vs green coloring
description: The figure is split into a left and a right panel by a dashed vertical line. Each panel shows photos of two similar black birds, Concept A and Concept B, feeding into frozen-VLM black boxes marked with snowflakes. On the left, a peach scroll prompt reads 'Describe the given image.' and goes to both VLMs independently. Both birds get the same peach attribute boxes: Black plumage, Black wings, Black head. The label 'Independently obtained' appears in red. On the right, a green scroll prompt asks 'What is different about image B compared to A?'. Both images go into one VLM, which outputs green boxes with distinct cues: Black eye, Thick beak, Shaggy feathers. A dashed horizontal line runs along the bottom. Below it, a dark-red 'Relation-agnostic Personalization System' box, labeled as failing, sits opposite a dark-green 'Our Relation-aware Personalization System' box, labeled as resolving ambiguity. A query image of a raven, with the question 'Is <concept B> in this image?', sits at the bottom left.
caption: Illustration of why relations matter. Left: When VLM describes each concept independently, it produces salient yet generic attributes shared across confusable concepts, leading to ambiguity. Right: When VLM is conditioned on the inter-concept relation (e.g., asking what differs between candidates), it can elicit discriminative cues that ease recognition even under fine-grained setting.
abstract: Training-free personalization adapts a frozen vision-language model (VLM) to recognize user-defined concepts from only a few exemplars by retrieving concept entries at inference time. While recent retriever-based methods enrich each concept with descriptive evidence, they largely treat concepts in isolation, so the retrieved information can be plausible yet non-discriminative, especially when the personalized concept set contains highly confusable, fine-grained categories. We argue that personalization is inherently relational: correct recognition depends on the specific distinctions between a concept and its nearest alternatives. To this end, we propose ReCoG, a Relational Concept Graph for retrieval-augmented personalization. ReCoG represents concepts as nodes and augments them with directed edges that explicitly capture discriminative cues between concept pairs, elicited by a frozen VLM during database construction. At inference, ReCoG retrieves a shortlist and resolves ambiguity via explicit pairwise comparisons conditioned on the corresponding relational edges, selecting the concept that consistently wins against competing candidates. We also introduce FINGER benchmark to test personalized recognition on confusable concept sets. Across FINGER, ReCoG substantially outperforms prior methods, with the largest gains in the most confusable regimes. ReCoG also achieves consistently best performance on established personalization benchmarks including captioning and VQA, confirming that relational evidence is broadly beneficial beyond fine-grained settings.
